explanation: Fires on the preposition introducing the agent or source after a passive or nominalized action verb, mostly 'by' (as in 'published by', 'appointed by', 'selected by', 'endorsed by'), and also 'from'/'to' in grant or transfer frames ('support from', 'status from'). It is strongest when the next word names an organization or person. Weaker on 'the' after 'by', on 'alleged that', and on similar words linking an action to its actor.
No common thread. Strong activations land on unrelated tokens in prose, code, JSON, SQL, email sign-offs ('Regards,'), Russian, and medical word-pieces ('extraint|estinal', 'B|cl').

Fires most strongly on '.org' in mozilla.org URLs. Otherwise it responds moderately to mid-word subword pieces, especially after 'Ren'/'Re'/'H'/'N' prefixes ('Ren|al', 'ren|in', 'H|un', 'N|oun'), and weakly to the middle digits of years and numbers ('19[9]2').

Fires on a subword token starting with 'w' or 'sw'/'tw' that begins a word or a word-piece: '-w' in 'award-winner'/'title-winner'/'recently-wed', ' w' in 'wok'/'worth'/'waltz', ' sw' in 'swine'/'swarms'/'swaths', 'W' in 'MagickWand'/'Wishlist'. Other initial consonant pieces ('sh', 'est', 'Brit') give weak responses.

Fires on the object slot right after a verb or preposition, most often the article 'a'/'an'/'such a' or a light verb such as 'use'/'access' after 'to' ('prefer to use', 'blew £183m on a', 'the wrong name for a'). These are typically spots where a generic noun phrase is about to follow. The token is less important than this 'start of object NP' position in informal or explanatory prose.

A mixture. It fires on completion pieces in the middle of words (echoc|ardi|ography, arr|hythm|ias, AFF|IRM|ED), on boilerplate in copyright/license headers ('Crytek Group', 'Dropbox, Inc', 'hereby granted', 'version 3 of'), and on assorted prose tokens, with no clear shared feature.

Fires on word-internal stem or affix pieces in non-English European languages (German, Scandinavian, Hungarian, Finnish, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Albanian), e.g. 'Wall|on|ie', 'af|ghan|ischen', 'naturl|igt|vis', 'Prants|us|maa'. Often these are pieces of borrowed or derived words. It fires weakly on CJK text and does not fire on English.

Go source-file preamble tokens: 'build' in '// +build' constraints, and 'import'/'package' just after a license or generated-code header. Weaker on other Go/Kubernetes code tokens (github.com, vendor, go install) and on the year digits in '// Copyright 201X'.

Fires on the function word introducing a role or purpose phrase: 'as' / 'as a' / 'as the' after 'used/served/employed', and 'for' in legal counsel lines ('Name, City, for appellant/defendant'). It also fires on the token opening a description slot, as in '@param ... The URL' or '@category'.

Fires on words about money and finance ('ticket price', 'weaker pound', 'Senate Finance', 'funds', 'dollar paid', 'afford', 'money', 'prices', 'BET'). It also fires moderately on nearby tokens in money or quantity contexts, such as 'per month', 'at an average' and counts of people.

Mostly fires on function words and adverbs right after a subject noun phrase in expository sentences, such as 'are', 'were', 'have', 'may', 'commonly', 'usually', 'originally', 'show' and 'who'. It also has unrelated code and number activations (virt_domain, getStatusLine, '95), so the core is loose.

Identifier components in code after a namespace or member-access separator, such as '.Nonnull', '.PublicKey', 'setLocation|RelativeTo', 'didFinish|Launching', 'android:text', '<Select'. The marked token is the second or later piece of a qualified API name or camelCase method in Java, Python, ObjC, Go, PHP or XML. It does not fire on prose.

A mixture. It fires on German function words and word endings ('bei der', 'gegen die', 'aufeinanderfol|genden'), Spanish/Portuguese verb endings, a few English tokens ('The function', 'ability of'), and code identifiers, with no clear shared trigger beyond a loose sense of word-grammar or language talk.

Programming and software-design vocabulary in technical discussions: 'low-level', 'overload', 'black-box', 'Implementor', 'implementation', 'backwards compatibility', 'functional', and code comment markers '//'. It fires inside code or on technical terms in prose about code; non-software text gives little.

Fires on a head noun naming what kind of thing an entity is, as in 'X is a ... [noun]' or 'the [company]': 'technology', 'mollusk', 'antibody', 'company', 'camera', 'cooler', 'footballer', 'politician', 'License', plus Japanese nouns for 'technology/product/existence'. The peak is a Japanese example, and many activations are weak.

No clear shared trigger. It fires on a broad mix of mid-name or mid-word pieces (Ara|uc|ania, V|erc|elli, H|oh|man), punctuation in references, 'in' in degree phrases ('MA in creative writing'), 'Atari 7800', 'https://' and more. Likely a positional or generic feature.

Two strong patterns. One is 'yards' (and 'tackles', 'starts') in American-football stat lines ('for 172 yards'). The other is 'to' in patent boilerplate 'The present invention relates (generally) to'. It also fires on scattered tokens in scientific or technical text.

No clear common trigger. Activations include 'ED' in 'UNITED STATES' case captions, subword pieces of technical or chemical words ('isoflur|ane', 'thr|usters', 'cesare|an'), 'be' in 'powers that be', and pieces of URLs or code identifiers.

Coordinators and list connectors joining two items in names, titles and boilerplate: 'and'/'&' in organization, law-firm and title names ('Evaluation and Research', 'Cooley & Allen', 'permissions and limitations'), plus 'or', 'including' and 'well'. Strongest when the two items form a fixed phrase or proper name.

Fires mainly on soft hyphens (U+00AD) inside hyphenated words ('mis­|lead'), and on the second piece of compounds split across tokens ('Way|f|aring', 'Pipe|f|itters', 'Wet’s|uw|et’en'). Other activations are weak and scattered.

Mainly the 'phosph' piece of biochemistry words ('phosphatase', 'cyclophosphamide') and other mid-word pieces of protein or enzyme names ('transf|err|in', 'integr|in', 'chymot|ry|psin'). A second, separate pattern is the 'Ste' that starts personal names ('Stevie', 'Steiker', 'Steptoe') and the first piece of other proper names.
